Black holes might split in two under extreme conditions, theoretical calculations suggest, offering physicists a way to explore the limits of our understanding of gravity. Two black holes can collide and merge into one. But could a single black hole divide into two smaller ones that go their separate ways? Reversing a merger might sound straightforward, but the rules governing black holes make it difficult. One obstacle is entropy, a measure of how many different microscopic arrangements can give a physical system the same overall properties. Think of rolling two dice. Several combinations produce a total of seven, but only two ones produce a total of two. Entropy captures a similar distinction between an overall result and the different underlying arrangements that can produce it. More possible arrangements mean higher entropy. For an ordinary black hole that is not rotating, two smaller black holes would have less combined entropy than the original. That makes splitting thermodynamically unfavorable. The usual requirement of thermodynamics is that the total entropy of an isolated system should stay the same or increase, rather than decrease. Whether black holes can split is the subject of “When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies,” a theoretical study published in Physical Review D . The unusual title describes what a split would look like through time. A black hole’s outer boundary, called its horizon, would trace a trouser-like shape, with one section dividing into two “legs.” “In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen”, says Francesco Sannino, a co-author and professor of physics at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark. Sannino’s co-authors are Giacomo Cacciapaglia, a Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS) researcher at the Laboratoire de Physique Théorique et Hautes Énergies, a joint laboratory of CNRS and Sorbonne Université in Paris, and Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark. Their calculations suggest that rapid rotation could offer a loophole in the thermodynamic barrier. A spinning black hole might be able to divide under conditions that would make splitting unfavorable for a nonrotating one. “But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate,” says Francesco Sannino. The researchers also explore theories with additional dimensions of space. Within these theories, physicists already know of black-hole-like objects that can become unstable and begin to break apart. Under some of these conditions, splitting can be thermodynamically favorable, particularly when one resulting black hole is much smaller than the other. Even then, showing that entropy permits a split does not establish that the process will actually happen. The possibilities also extend to primordial black holes, hypothetical objects that could have formed in the early universe. “We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein’s theory, and we are working to quantify this. We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers,” says Francesco Sannino. Researchers have discovered how pressure can unlock hidden superconducting properties in a complex quantum material. Applying intense pressure to an unusual quantum material can transform how it conducts electricity, allowing superconductivity to spread throughout its three-dimensional structure at temperatures roughly three times higher than normal. Researchers also found a sevenfold increase in the number of electrons participating in superconductivity. The discovery comes from a team led by Zurab Guguchia at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland. Their findings, published in Nature Communications , provide new insight into how superconductivity might be strengthened and eventually achieved under more practical conditions. Tantalum disulfide has a simple chemical composition but a remarkably complex electronic structure. It consists of extremely thin atomic layers that behave differently as temperatures fall. “Its chemical formula sounds very simple: for every tantalum atom there are two sulfur atoms,” says Guguchia. “But inside it is an enormously complex material with almost paradoxical properties.” When produced in a particular way, the material contains alternating layers with two distinct atomic arrangements. Both conduct electricity at higher temperatures, but cooling causes one to become an insulator while the other becomes superconducting, carrying current without electrical resistance. “This means that the electronic properties of these two layers behave in completely opposite ways,” Guguchia explains. Initially, superconductivity remains confined to individual conducting layers because the insulating layers obstruct electron movement between them. But cooling the material to just over 1 kelvin (about −458°F) produces a dramatic change. “Suddenly the entire material becomes superconducting, so the insulating layers also become conductive and take part in superconductivity,” Guguchia says. Instead of remaining restricted to separate planes, superconductivity extends throughout the crystal in three dimensions. Scientists knew that applying pressure could raise the temperature at which this transition occurs, but the underlying mechanisms were unclear. The PSI team investigated how compression affects the material’s electrons and the interactions between its layers. The researchers subjected tantalum disulfide to pressures several hundred times greater than those inside a typical car tire. Compression brought the superconducting layers closer together, reducing the disruptive effect of the insulating layers. It also allowed previously localized electrons within the insulating layers to participate in superconductivity. “Due to these effects, high pressure causes tantalum disulfide to become superconducting in all three dimensions at temperatures approximately three times higher.” Measurements also revealed a sevenfold increase in the number of electrons participating in superconductivity. “So, pressure not only raises the temperature at which superconductivity can occur, but also changes the very nature of the superconducting state,” the researcher explained. “It alters the way electrons pair up and move together through the material, resulting in a more robust form of superconductivity.” To investigate these changes, the team used muon spin spectroscopy, a technique that detects magnetic conditions inside materials. Muons are elementary particles similar to electrons but approximately 200 times heavier. Although they survive for only a few millionths of a second, their sensitivity to local magnetic fields makes them especially useful for studying superconductors. “Since muons are exceptionally sensitive probes for magnetic and superconducting properties, we can gain unique insights into quantum materials here at PSI,” Guguchia says. PSI operates the Swiss Muon Source SμS, the world’s most powerful muon source. By combining muon measurements with other techniques, the researchers examined how pressure changes electron behavior at extremely low temperatures. Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, eliminating conduction losses and associated waste heat. However, the extreme cooling requirements of most superconducting materials have limited their applications. They are currently used in specialized systems, including the powerful magnets at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. “Currently, research is being conducted worldwide on novel, unconventional superconductors that exhibit robust superconductivity even at higher temperatures or in strong external magnetic fields,” Guguchia says. Although tantalum disulfide still requires extremely low temperatures, the findings demonstrate how pressure can alter electron pairing and strengthen superconductivity. These insights could help researchers develop materials that operate closer to room temperature and under ordinary atmospheric pressure. “By investigating important quantum materials, we want to uncover the fundamental mechanisms underlying superconductivity,” Guguchia says. “This will allow us to find ways to optimize the temperatures at which superconductivity occurs.” Future experiments at PSI could provide even more detailed measurements. Through the planned IMPACT project (IMPACT stands for: Isotope and Muon Production using Advanced Cyclotron and Target technologies), the institute expects to develop muon beams hundreds of times more powerful than those currently available. Together with the Muoniverse research initiative, the upgrade will expand opportunities to investigate superconducting quantum materials. “We are already looking forward to the new perspectives these two developments will offer,” Guguchia concludes. “Especially for work on superconducting quantum materials, this opens up unimagined experimental possibilities.” Reference: “Competing quantum orders in 6R-TaS2 revealed by pressure” by V. Beeswax combs, stored pollen, and substances produced by the bees themselves helped suppress harmful bacteria and fungi while supporting beneficial microbial communities. “As we travel closer to the hive center, the antimicrobial defenses became more targeted, with wax comb, stored pollen, and the bee’s own bodies helping to filter out harmful bacteria and fungi, while encouraging helpful species,” said Fernandes, a 2026 NSW Tall Young Poppy Award recipient. “We already know honey, beeswax and propolis have antimicrobial properties independently. But what came as a surprise was how these materials were placed in the hive wasn’t random, but organized. The hive’s antimicrobial properties worked together to protect the eggs and larvae, as well as the fermented pollen the bees consume.” For the study, published in ISME Communications , scientists examined 24 honey bee colonies across five apiaries at Tocal College in New South Wales, Australia. They analyzed the chemical composition and antimicrobial properties of honey, pollen, beeswax, and propolis. They also investigated microbes living in the bees’ digestive systems and tested the antimicrobial activity of their tissues and secretions. The researchers found that many microorganisms in hive materials likely originated from floral nectar. Colonies located closer to native bushland also showed measurable differences in chemical defenses compared with those near agricultural land. These differences suggest that the plants available to foraging bees influence the protective properties of the materials they bring home. “This shows healthy hives depend on and are influenced by healthy ecosystems. Land clearing and intensive farming could be quietly eroding the bees’ natural defenses. This builds a strong case for protecting diverse flowering habitats that support healthy hives,” said co-author Elizabeth Frost, Technical Specialist Bees at the NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD). The hive’s protective system was generally more effective against bacteria than fungi. Researchers suggest this imbalance may reflect the greater threat posed by certain bacterial infections. One example is American foulbrood, a highly contagious disease that kills honeybee larvae and can destroy entire colonies. “There are direct threats to bee populations such as the varroa mite, but many don’t realize the indirect threats: the shrinking of healthy ecosystems has a domino effect. Landscapes with diverse plant species can increase the bees’ chances of being resilient to disease.” The findings also raise questions about other colony-building insects. Although the study focused on European honey bees, Fernandes hopes to investigate whether Australian native stingless bees have comparable nest-based defenses and whether similar systems occur in other social insects. “I’d love to see if other social insects such as native stingless bees, ants, and termites, which also build incredibly complex homes, also have the same system,” Fernandes said. Reference: “Spatially organized chemical defences shape microbial communities in honey bee colonies” by Kenya E Fernandes, Aviva Levina, Elizabeth A Frost and Dee A Carter, 19 October 2026, ISME Communications . title: Earliest evidence of cannabis use found in ancient Siberian tomb
content: Archaeologists have found the earliest evidence of people consuming cannabis for psychoactive purposes in a tomb dating back almost 3,000 years, according to a new study. Researchers found preserved cannabis seeds and human hair at the monumental elite tomb in southern Siberia , lead study author Gino Caspari, a researcher at the University of Bern, Switzerland, told CNN. “There is a lot of speculation about prehistoric use of plant-based drugs, but through this find we are actually able to show that there is a basis to it,” he said. The tomb is located in the Uyuk Valley and contains the remains of various high-status individuals. Caspari and colleagues have been working there since 2017, uncovering evidence that the tomb dated from 2,800 years ago, during the earliest Scythian period. “These were nomadic horse-back riders known for their skill of shooting from horseback and for their exquisite gold items,” he said. At the site, Caspari and his colleagues spotted small black dots in the tomb and were able to identify them as cannabis seeds. They eventually recovered more than 1,400 of them and used radiocarbon dating to ascertain that they had been deposited around 2,800 years ago. They also found preserved human hair, which they tested using a mass spectrometer. “Surviving plant remains which are almost 3,000 years old are extremely rare,” Caspari told CNN, as they are generally poorly preserved. “It is even rarer to find them in combination with human soft tissue like hair, which essentially allows (us) to drug test a person who has been dead for three millennia.” Analysis revealed that the hair tested positive for THC (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol), the primary psychoactive compound in cannabis, as well as cannabinol, a chemical compound produced when THC is exposed to air. “That was just an amazing moment,” said Caspari, who said that the discovery adds to our understanding of the history of the consumption of cannabis. Up to now, scientists had found evidence that cannabis was cultivated in East Asia at least 6,000 years ago, probably for its oil-rich seeds, according to a statement from the researchers. Evidence of the plant’s use for its mind-altering effects had previously been found as far back as 2,500 years ago, including in ritual practices in Central Asia, the statement adds. “The cannabis use has to be seen in a ritual context in the tomb and may be connected to shamanistic beliefs,” Caspari told CNN. “Since we have dozens of sacrificed horses and some potential human sacrifices it might also have been used to sedate the victims before something bad happened to them — but we cannot prove that,” he said. “Surprisingly little is known about the deep time cultural history of this important crop. For example, we are not even sure what truly wild cannabis actually looks like,” he added. “Now we have at least 3,000 years of psychoactive cannabis consumption on the Eurasian continent and it seems that at this point it was already spread from China to Europe,” he said. “We think this provides a cultural anchor point for current debates on legalization and medical use of the plant.” Caspari added that the team are now sequencing the ancient DNA of the seeds they found at the site. “Having well-preserved plant DNA is even rarer than having plant remains and this is the oldest preserved cannabis DNA,” he said. “In the next few years our team will probably rewrite part of the domestication history of cannabis.” Roger Forshaw, an honorary lecturer in biomedical Egyptology at the University of Manchester, England, who was not involved in the study, told CNN that the research “provides some fascinating insights into the use of cannabis among early Iron Age communities in Central Asia, a practice for which direct archaeological evidence has previously been scarce.” The fact that chemical traces of cannabis were found in the hair “provides direct molecular evidence of cannabis use and supports the interpretation that it formed part of the funerary rituals,” he said. “Although we cannot be certain how the plant was administered or precisely what role it played in the burial rituals, the discovery adds considerably to our understanding of the use of psychoactive plants in ancient societies,” Forshaw added. The study was published Thursday in the journal Science .

title: These rare killer whales are threatened by shipping noise. AI is turning down the din
content: Seventy-six orcas arrived in the Salish Sea in September — the last of an endangered population known as southern resident killer whales. Every year, the few score left enter Admiralty Inlet and head toward Puget Sound, Washington, which they’ll move in and out of from late summer until early winter. One of the most endangered whales, and one of few orca communities that rely on fish, they make the journey into the fjords to hunt Chinook salmon. But their ears are ringing. Noise pollution from heavily trafficked maritime shipping lanes affects their ability to hunt, communicate and echolocate. Moreover, vessels pose a deadly collision risk. Scientists didn’t realize the southern resident was a different, genetically distinct group of orcas to the more populous Bigg’s killer whale until the 1970s. The first survey , conducted in 1974, found just 71 whales, peaking at 97 in 1996 but declining to 79 in 2001. The southern resident was listed as endangered in 2005. “Underwater noise is a pervasive threat,” said Rachel Aronson, program director of Quiet Sound, an initiative within Maritime Blue, which promotes sustainable maritime practices. “When it’s loud underwater, it gets harder for (southern resident killer whales) to find food. Sometimes they will hunt and miss, so they’ve expended energy but gotten nothing back. Sometimes they just forgo hunting, which is a problem, especially if they’re a female who is building up to a pregnancy or nursing a baby.” A 2024 study found that for every one decibel increase in maximum noise level, females were 58% less likely to pursue prey, and males and females were 12.5% less likely to capture prey. Washington is a trade-dependent state, where 40% of jobs are tied to international commerce , so balancing maritime industries with wildlife conservation is a delicate act. Following a similar model to its Canadian counterpart, the Echo Program, in 2022 Quiet Sound introduced a voluntary slow down program for ships along a 20-mile stretch coming into Seattle, Tacoma and Everett, Washington’s three largest ports. Slower ships mean less noise pollution. Aronson said so far this season there’s been a 73% participation rate, and underwater noise has reduced by as much as 50% since the voluntary slow-down was introduced. But tracking the whereabouts of killer whales — specifically southern residents — to keep them from harm remains a challenge. Ahead of the whales’ migration to Puget Sound this year, Quiet Sound teamed up with SMRU Consulting and Microsoft to launch an AI-powered acoustic buoy to listen out for them. SMRU Consulting, a subsidiary of the University of St Andrews, in the UK, has developed a series of smart buoys since 2014. They have been used to monitor wildlife in Scotland, the US East Coast and the Pacific Northwest in areas where human presence may cause a disturbance. Cormac Booth, managing director, said that while marine acoustic monitoring has been around for decades, the gap between data collection and analysis was once many months. As technology has evolved, “we’ve moved away from that after-the-fact archival approach,” he said. Today, “it’s about being able to provide reliable insights of what is happening now, allowing people to make decisions now.” In July 2025, SMRU Consulting and Microsoft entered a partnership to create and test whether AI on board a buoy could correctly identify killer whale and humpback whale calls. “Underwater monitoring produces far more audio than people can review manually. The speed of processing this amount of data in near-real time is where AI helps most,” said Juan Lavista Ferres, chief data scientist and corporate vice president of Microsoft, and lab director of the Microsoft AI for Good Lab. Microsoft equipped an SMRU buoy with Water SPARROW (Solar-Powered Acoustic and Remote Recording Observation Watch), an aquatic version of its wildlife monitoring AI. The open-source edge computing solution was launched in 2024 and is already used in camera traps to processes images, audio and sensor data for species identification. Working with Quiet Sound, Microsoft and SMRU Consulting launched their Communications Acoustics Buoy (CAB) in July and positioned it in the Haro Strait, spanning the Canada-US border. “This area you can get the biggest bang for your buck for southern residents,” said Jason Wood, principal scientist and deputy director of technology at SMRU Consulting. The buoy features three hydrophones anchored underwater, with Microsoft’s system floating in the buoy and SMRU’s analysis system below the surface. Wood said Microsoft and SMRU are engaged in a “bake off” to see if the AI or SMRU’s system will detect southern resident killer whale signals with the greatest accuracy. “The results so far are encouraging,” said Ferres. “As the team has adapted the models to the underwater sounds of Puget Sound and collected more field data, false positives have decreased to a level where Water SPARROW can now operate as a functional detection system.” Wood said due to the risk of false positives, the buoy had not begun sending its finding to WRAS (Whale Report Alert System), a conservation tool managed by Ocean Wise to alert mariners of whale locations and prevent ship strikes. This could change. WRAS is multimodal, relying on human sightings, thermal imaging and hydrophones to composite a map of whale locations. Commercial marine pilots receive a text alert when a phone is within 10 nautical miles of a whale sighting, said Aronson. “We want mariners to have this real-time awareness and be able to check in advance of their arrival somewhere,” she said. “It can take these large vessels five miles to slow down, so having this awareness region-wide is really important.” Wood acknowledged that each detection method has its limitations: human sightings are predominantly during the daytime; thermal imaging is limited mostly to the surface; and hydrophones work when whales are calling. But he was hopeful that introducing these disparate datasets to an AI in the future could yield better species detection — and more actionable data. Ferres said one of Microsoft’s goals is to provide more information on the seasonal patterns of killer whales to support wildlife management and conservationists — a model that could be extended to other species in the Salish Sea. He also said a goal is to make Water SPARROW open source, like its landbound predecessor, so it can be put in the hands of more conservationists and installed on other compatible buoys. “Given the endangered state of this population, it’s not a matter of whether these AI-enabled buoys can be rolled out more broadly, but when,” said Ferres. “Conservation of these whales depends on it.”

title: A pizza topping that divides the world
content:
In the 1960s, a chef in Canada created a pizza topping that swept the globe. But there are good scientific reasons why is it so widely loved – and hated.
It's not Hawaii you should thank – or indeed blame, depending on your viewpoint.
The man popularly credited with giving the world the ham and pineapple pizza was neither Hawaiian, nor in fact Italian.
Sam Panopoulos was a Greek immigrant to Canada who ran a restaurant with his brothers in the city of Chatham, Ontario. Panopoulos had recently visited Naples – the birthplace of pizza – and was inspired to start adding the Italian staple to the restaurant's usual line-up of burgers and pancakes. But what to put on it?
Panopoulos pushed past the then-standard toppings such as mushroom and pepperoni, turning to south-of-the-border inspiration – in this case, the sweet-and-sour flavours which characterised America's take on Chinese food. On top of a cheese-and-tomato-sauce pizza base, he spread canned pineapple and sliced ham, perhaps influenced by the sweet-and-salty taste of Chinese dishes pairing pork and pineapple.
Depending on which side of the divide you stand, a classic dish, or a culinary crime, was born.
Few foods divide as dramatically as ham and pineapple pizza. In many parts of the US, UK and Australasia, few pizza menus seem complete without it. In Italy, however, the pairing is widely considered an abomination . In 2026, Australia's Fair Work Commission heard that one Italian chef refused to put the topping on pizzas he was asked to cook because he "considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on pizza is an insult to his culture ".
The controversial topping has even led to international disputes between world leaders and diplomatic interventions . But why is it so divisive?
"I guess you might call it a fusion food, before the term became popular. And, of course, sweet is the most-liked taste, so it is an easy win in that sense," says Charles Spence, an experimental psychologist who studies how our different senses affect our experience of food at the University of Oxford.
Panopoulos' pairing of processed ham and pineapple coincided with the release of the Tropical Recipe Book by Australian food processing company Golden Circle . They were – surprise, surprise – a major producer of canned pineapple, and the book's cover shows pineapple rings gracing a cooked ham.
A decade before, a TV cook introduced post-war Germany to a treat called Toast Hawaii, consisting of a pineapple ring, cooked ham and sliced cheese, all cooked under the grill. This may have in fact been a German reworking of the Grilled Spamwich, a spam-and-pineapple recipe which had come over with US soldiers stationed in West Germany after World War Two. All combined the characteristic sweetness of pineapple with the salty, umami foil of processed pork.
Pork and pineapple is, of course, not the only fruit and meat pairing in world cuisine. In France, duck is paired with a sweet orange sauce. Iranian pilaf mixes lamb with pomegranate. American Thanksgiving dinners would not be the same without cranberry sauce accompanying the traditional turkey, or the marshmallows and yams.
So why would that work? As the recent explosion in salted-caramel treats has shown us, salty and sweet flavours intrinsically work together. It creates something known as " flavour-layering ". This layering causes the brain to react with positive signals, sensing the combination of sweetness – and its carbohydrate fuel – and salt, which is vital for bodily functions.
And pineapple certainly packs a punch in the sweetness department. About 12 - 15% of a pineapple's weight comes from sugar – mainly sucrose, but also glucose and fructose. Yet pineapples are also fairly acidic, with a pH of between 3-4 , depending on the variety (for context, lemon juice has a pH of between 2-3.) Much like that in a can of cola – which is also surprisingly acidic at pH 2-3 – the sugar offsets the tartness and makes it palatable, even enjoyable.
Some people, however, are more sensitive to certain tastes than others. Genetic factors are thought to play a role in how much we each enjoy sour tastes , and scientists have found that people who carry variants of a specific gene called TAS2R38 can be more or less sensitive to bitter compounds. Similarly, our liking for sweet tastes is also influenced by our genes and can affect how much sugary food we eat. It is likely, perhaps, that whether someone likes pineapple on their pizza or not, comes down to their genes.
This makes even more sense when you consider what happens when pineapple is cooked.
"There are many chemical reactions when pineapple is being heated, as it contains a lot of sugars and organic acids," says Zhimin Xu, a food scientist who studies the volatile chemicals that contribute to flavour at Louisiana State University Agricultural Center in Baton Rouge, US. He and his colleagues have studied exactly what happens to pineapple when it is cooked at different temperatures .
"At mild heating temperature, its fruity aroma is quickly released, but its intensity gets lower and lower with increases of heating temperature and time, while the bread-like aroma increases during heating," he says. "Heated pineapple also has less sweet-and-sour taste compared with fresh-cut pineapple."
But it's when pineapple is heated at high temperatures that things start to get interesting. Most frozen and shop-bought pizzas cooked in domestic ovens at home spend 10-20 minutes in temperatures of 200C-220C (392F-428F), but in a woodfired pizza oven, temperatures can reach more than 500C (932F) and the pizza needs less than a couple of minutes.
Xu and his colleagues found that at temperatures between 200C-225C (392F-437F), the balance of volatile compounds – those that easily become vapour at room temperature and so often contribute to odours and flavours in food – started to change dramatically.
